theme: Escalate wisely: cascades, signals and ownership

questions.concept: Real-time brevity in assistive scene description for blind users
questions.question: You are building a phone-camera feature that describes surroundings aloud for blind users while they walk. Early testers say the descriptions are 'accurate but useless'. Which change most directly addresses the core problem?
options: Lead with short, prioritised cues about obstacles and changes in the scene, and let users ask for more detail
Use a larger vision model so descriptions capture more objects and finer visual detail
Add a confidence score to every description so users know how reliable each one is
Let users pick a preferred narration voice and speaking speed from a settings menu
questions.explanation: For a user in motion, a description is only useful if it arrives in time and tells them what matters for the next few steps. 'Accurate but useless' signals the content is complete but badly prioritised and too slow to consume by ear. Leading with brief, safety-relevant cues and offering detail on demand fits the context of use: audio is serial, so every extra word delays the important one.
rationales: Correct: it fixes prioritisation and length, the real failure for audio consumed while walking, and keeps detail available on demand.
More detail makes descriptions longer and slower to hear; the problem is relevance and timing, not missing objects.
Confidence scores add words without telling the user what to do next; they do not fix the priority problem.
Voice and speed are comfort settings; a faster voice reading the wrong content first is still unhelpful.
questions.interview_tip: Accessibility prompts test whether you design from the user's context of use rather than from model capability. Strong answers name the constraint (serial audio, user in motion) before proposing a solution.

questions.concept: Converting saved recipes into an actionable meal plan
questions.question: A recipe app finds that users save about 20 recipes a month but cook fewer than two of them. The team wants to raise 'recipes cooked'. Which product bet best targets the most likely gap between saving and cooking?
options: Recommend more personalised recipes on the home feed so users find dishes they love
Let users drag saved recipes into a weekly plan that builds a combined grocery list they can order
Add a badge and streak for every recipe a user marks as cooked in a week
Add step-by-step video to every recipe so cooking feels easier to follow
questions.explanation: Saving is cheap intent; cooking needs a decision about when to cook and the ingredients on hand. Users already save plenty, so discovery is not the bottleneck. A plan-plus-grocery-list flow removes the two biggest frictions between intent and action: scheduling and shopping. It also creates a natural commerce hook for the business.
rationales: More recommendations increase saves, which are already high; the drop-off happens after saving.
Correct: it tackles planning and ingredient friction, the steps that actually sit between saving a recipe and cooking it.
Gamification rewards the outcome without removing the obstacles, and invites false 'cooked' taps.
Videos help during cooking, but most users never reach the stove; the gap appears earlier in the journey.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like candidates who locate the exact step where the funnel breaks before ideating. Saying 'saves are high, so discovery is not the problem' shows disciplined reasoning.

questions.concept: Fit guidance from past purchases to cut size-related returns
questions.question: An Indian fashion marketplace sees 30% of apparel orders returned, and 'size didn't fit' is the top reason. Sizes vary widely between brands. Which feature most directly reduces these returns?
options: Offer free return pickup within 24 hours so the return experience feels painless
Show a standard size chart on every product page with measurements in centimetres
Recommend a size for each brand based on items the shopper kept versus returned in the past
Show more model photos from different angles so shoppers can judge the cut better
questions.explanation: The root cause is inconsistent sizing across brands, so a generic size chart does not resolve the user's real question: 'what size am I in this brand?'. Purchase history (kept vs returned) is a strong, cheap signal of true fit, and mapping it brand by brand answers that question directly. It reduces returns at the decision point instead of making returns easier.
rationales: Easier returns improve satisfaction but likely increase return rates; it treats the symptom, not the cause.
Size charts exist on most sites already and require shoppers to measure themselves, which few do; they do not resolve brand inconsistency.
Correct: it uses the user's own fit history to answer the brand-specific size question that drives returns.
Photos help judge style and cut, but the top return reason is size, which photos cannot resolve.
questions.interview_tip: A strong answer ties the solution to the stated root cause and to a data asset the company already owns. Mentioning a guardrail such as keep-rate per recommended size earns extra credit.

questions.concept: Showing expected earnings before gig workers accept a task
questions.question: Delivery partners on a quick-commerce app reject 35% of offered orders, which slows deliveries. Interviews show partners don't know what an order will pay until it is finished. What should the PM prioritise first?
options: Penalise partners whose acceptance rate falls below a set threshold each week
Raise the base pay per order across the board to make every order attractive
Hide the order details until acceptance so partners cannot reject long trips
Show estimated pay, distance and time on the offer screen before the partner accepts
questions.explanation: Partners are making decisions under uncertainty, so they reject defensively to avoid orders that may turn out to be poor value. Showing expected earnings, distance and time lets them accept with confidence and is the cheapest test of whether uncertainty drives rejections. Penalties or blanket pay rises address the symptom and either hurt trust or cost a lot without proving the cause.
rationales: Penalties raise acceptance short-term but damage trust and supply retention, and they ignore the stated cause.
Blanket pay rises are expensive and still leave partners unable to judge individual orders.
Hiding details makes the uncertainty worse and tends to increase cancellations after acceptance.
Correct: it directly removes the information gap partners identified and is cheap to test.
questions.interview_tip: Two-sided marketplace questions test whether you treat suppliers as users with their own pains. Strong candidates fix the information gap before reaching for penalties or money.

questions.concept: Evaluating a free-delivery threshold raise on per-customer profit and retention
questions.question: A quick-commerce app raised its free-delivery threshold from ₹199 to ₹299. Two weeks later, average order value is up 18%, orders per customer are down 12%, and revenue is flat. What is the best way to judge whether the change worked?
options: Call it a success because AOV rose sharply, which signals customers are building larger baskets
Compare contribution profit per customer and the retention of affected cohorts over the coming weeks
Call it a failure because order frequency fell, and frequency drives habit and long-term retention
Call it neutral because revenue is flat, so the change had no meaningful business effect
questions.explanation: A threshold change shifts several metrics in opposite directions, so no single one gives the verdict. Fewer, bigger orders can be more profitable because delivery cost per order is largely fixed, but lower frequency might signal churn that shows up later. The right lens is contribution profit per customer over time, plus cohort retention to catch delayed damage.
rationales: AOV alone ignores the drop in order frequency and any customers who quietly stopped ordering.
Correct: it combines unit economics with a retention check, which is what decides whether the trade-off pays off.
Lower frequency is a warning sign, but fewer, larger orders can still be healthier economically; it needs profit and retention data.
Flat revenue can hide a big change in profit, since delivery costs fall with fewer orders.
questions.interview_tip: Metric trade-off questions reward candidates who move from a vanity metric to the business outcome (profit per customer) and add a time dimension. Naming the cohort check shows maturity.

questions.concept: Primary success metric for a wishlist feature
questions.question: An e-commerce app launches a 'Save to wishlist' button. Which metric best captures whether the feature creates value for the business?
options: Total number of items added to wishlists per day across the app
Share of daily active users who tapped the wishlist button at least once
Share of wishlisted items that are purchased within 30 days of being saved
Average number of items each user keeps in their wishlist over time
questions.explanation: A wishlist is valuable if it helps users come back and buy what they wanted. Saved-to-purchased conversion within a fixed window ties the feature to the outcome, while counts of saves only measure activity. Pair it with a check that overall conversion did not fall, in case saving replaces buying now.
rationales: Adds per day measure engagement with the button, not whether the saves lead anywhere.
Adoption shows reach, but a feature can be widely tapped and still create no purchases.
Correct: it links the feature to downstream purchases within a defined window.
Large wishlists can mean users park items and never buy; size alone is ambiguous.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers want you to separate activity metrics from outcome metrics. Mentioning a guardrail against cannibalising immediate purchases signals strong judgment.

questions.concept: Separating push-driven from organic DAU
questions.question: A social app's DAU rose 9% this quarter, mostly after the growth team doubled daily push notifications. Leadership asks whether the product got healthier. What is the most useful next analysis?
options: Split DAU into push-attributed and organic sessions and track notification opt-out rates
Compare this quarter's DAU with the same quarter last year to remove seasonality
Survey a sample of users to ask whether they are enjoying the app more than before
Report the 9% DAU rise as the headline, since daily usage is the app's North Star
questions.explanation: Push notifications can manufacture visits without making the product more valuable, and they spend a limited resource: user tolerance. Separating push-driven from organic usage shows whether underlying demand changed, and opt-out or uninstall rates reveal the hidden cost. Healthy growth shows up in organic return visits.
rationales: Correct: it isolates organic demand and measures the cost of the extra notifications.
Seasonality is worth checking, but it does not answer whether the gain is just notification pressure.
Surveys are slow and unreliable for this; behavioural data can answer the question directly.
Headline DAU is exactly the number in doubt; reporting it without decomposition can mislead leadership.
questions.interview_tip: Expect 'is this growth real?' follow-ups in Meta-style execution rounds. Strong answers decompose the metric by source and name the long-term cost of the lever used.

questions.concept: Thinning auction density behind falling ad prices
questions.question: An ads marketplace sees revenue fall 10% while impressions and click-through rate are flat. Average cost per click dropped noticeably. What is the most likely driver to investigate first?
options: Users have become less interested in ads, so engagement with them is declining
Ad load increased, so users are seeing more ads and ignoring most of them
Fewer advertisers are competing in each auction, so winning bids and prices have fallen
A logging bug is double-counting impressions, so revenue per impression looks lower
questions.explanation: With impressions and CTR steady, clicks are steady too, so the revenue drop must come from price per click. In auction-based ads, price depends on how many advertisers compete: if budgets shrink or advertisers leave, second-price levels fall. The next step is to look at advertisers per auction and spend by advertiser segment.
rationales: Flat CTR shows user engagement with ads has not changed.
Impressions are flat, so ad load has not risen.
Correct: flat volume plus lower CPC points to weaker auction competition, i.e. demand-side pressure.
Double-counted impressions would show impressions rising, but they are flat.
questions.interview_tip: Root-cause questions reward decomposing revenue into volume and price before guessing. Knowing that auction prices depend on competition depth shows real ads fluency.

questions.concept: Shared advertiser budgets causing interference in ads tests
questions.question: You A/B test a new ad ranking model by splitting users 50/50. Treatment shows a 6% revenue lift. An analyst warns the true effect at full launch may be near zero. What is the most likely reason?
options: The sample is too small, so the 6% lift is probably a false positive from noise
Advertisers' fixed budgets are shared across both groups, so treatment may just pull spend from control
Users in treatment saw a novel ad layout, so the lift will fade as novelty wears off
Revenue is a heavy-tailed metric, so a few big advertisers may have skewed the comparison
questions.explanation: When advertisers have fixed budgets, treatment and control compete for the same money. A better model in treatment can spend budgets faster there, which inflates treatment and depresses control, even if total spend does not change at launch. Budget-split designs, which give each arm its own share of every advertiser's budget, avoid this interference.
rationales: A small sample could cause noise, but the analyst's point is structural bias that more data would not fix.
Correct: shared budgets violate the independence between arms, so the measured lift overstates the real effect.
Novelty affects user behaviour; it does not explain why the total effect would be zero.
Outliers add noise, but the warning concerns a systematic transfer of spend between arms.
questions.interview_tip: Interference questions separate strong experimenters from average ones. Naming the mechanism (shared budget) and the fix (budget-split or cluster design) is the bar.

questions.concept: Machine opens inflating email open-rate tests
questions.question: A D2C brand A/B tests two email subject lines and picks the winner by open rate. Many subscribers use mail apps that pre-load emails for privacy. What is the better primary metric?
options: Open rate, but only counting opens that happen within the first hour of sending
Unsubscribe rate, since a good subject line should keep subscribers on the list
Number of emails delivered successfully to the inbox rather than the spam folder
Click-through rate or downstream purchases from each email variant
questions.explanation: Privacy features in some mail apps load email content automatically, which records an 'open' whether or not a person read it. That makes open rate noisy and biased toward those clients. Clicks and purchases require real human action, so they measure what the subject line is meant to drive.
rationales: Automatic loads often happen right after delivery, so a time window does not remove them.
Unsubscribes are a useful guardrail but too rare and too indirect to pick a subject-line winner.
Deliverability matters, but both variants go to the same list; it does not measure persuasion.
Correct: clicks and purchases need real human action and reflect the business goal.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like candidates who question whether the metric is measured correctly before trusting a test. Mentioning instrumentation limits shows practical experience.

questions.concept: Number of practising dentists needed in Bengaluru
questions.question: Estimate roughly how many full-time dentists are needed to meet demand for dental visits in Bengaluru (population about 14 million).
options: About 200
About 2,000
About 20,000
About 200,000
questions.explanation: Demand side: 14M people x about 0.5 dental visits per person per year (many people rarely visit, some visit several times) = about 7M visits a year. Supply side: a dentist sees about 12 patients a day x 300 working days = 3,600 visits a year. 7M / 3,600 = about 2,000 dentists. Actual headcount may be higher because many clinics run below capacity, which is worth noting.
rationales: 200 dentists would need about 35,000 visits each a year, far above what one person can handle.
Correct: about 7M visits a year divided by about 3,600 visits per dentist gives roughly 2,000.
20,000 implies each dentist sees under 2 patients a day at 0.5 visits per person, which is too low for a full-time practice.
200,000 would be about one dentist per 70 residents, far beyond any realistic ratio.
questions.interview_tip: Show a demand-side and a supply-side build and sanity-check one against the other. Calling out assumptions you are least sure of (visit frequency) signals rigour.

questions.concept: Daily petrol consumed by two-wheelers in Bengaluru
questions.question: Estimate roughly how many litres of petrol two-wheelers in Bengaluru consume on a typical day. Assume about 10 million registered two-wheelers.
options: About 30,000 litres
About 300,000 litres
About 3 million litres
About 30 million litres
questions.explanation: Not every registered vehicle is used daily: assume about 60%, so 6M on the road. Average distance about 20 km a day; typical mileage about 45 km per litre, so about 0.45 litres per vehicle per day. 6M x 0.45 = about 2.7M litres, roughly 3 million litres a day.
rationales: 30,000 litres would be about 0.005 litres per active vehicle, under a quarter of a kilometre each.
300,000 litres means each active vehicle rides only about 2 km a day, too low for commuting use.
Correct: about 6M active vehicles x about 0.45 litres gives roughly 3M litres a day.
30 million litres would mean about 5 litres per active two-wheeler daily, over 200 km each.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers watch for an 'active share' adjustment instead of using the registered base directly. Clear units at each step make the method easy to follow.

questions.concept: Defending against platform-owner feature copying (Sherlocking)
questions.question: Your screen-recording app is a top seller on a major operating system's app store. Rumours say the OS maker will build basic screen recording into the next release. What is the strongest strategic response?
options: Cut the app's price sharply now to lock in as many users as possible before the release
Lobby the OS maker to drop the feature by highlighting your app's popularity on their store
Deepen into workflows the built-in tool won't serve, such as editing, team sharing and cross-platform use
Ignore the rumour, since built-in tools are usually basic and users rarely switch away
questions.explanation: When a platform owner bundles a basic version of your product, the basic use case becomes free for everyone. The defence is to move to value the platform is unlikely to build: advanced workflows, collaboration, and support for other platforms the owner will never serve. That keeps a segment willing to pay even after the default is free.
rationales: Price cuts compete against free and only delay the problem while hurting margins.
Platforms rarely drop features because a third party asks; this is not a strategy.
Correct: it moves the product to value the platform owner is unlikely to replicate.
Defaults are powerful; many casual users will switch to a free built-in tool.
questions.interview_tip: Platform-risk prompts test whether you understand defaults and bundling. Strong answers name what the platform owner won't build and why.

questions.concept: Choosing an expansion market by similarity to the home market
questions.question: An Indian UPI-based bill-payments app wants to expand abroad. Which market-selection logic is strongest for a first expansion?
options: Pick the country with the largest population, since it has the biggest addressable market
Pick the richest country, since higher incomes mean larger bill amounts and better fees
Pick the country where competitors are weakest, regardless of how payments work there
Pick a country with real-time account-to-account payments and similar bill-pay habits to India
questions.explanation: A first expansion should reuse as much of the existing product, playbook and partnerships as possible. A market with similar payment infrastructure and user behaviour lets the team transfer what it has learned and keeps the cost of failure low. Size and wealth matter later, once the company has proven it can expand.
rationales: Large population is attractive, but if payment rails differ, the product may need rebuilding from scratch.
Rich markets often have mature card-based systems and strong incumbents, which makes the product less differentiated.
Weak competition is helpful only if the product can work there; infrastructure fit comes first.
Correct: similar rails and habits maximise reuse of the product and playbook and lower risk.
questions.interview_tip: Market-entry answers are stronger when they score markets on 'right to win' as well as size. Explicit criteria and a sequencing argument signal strategic thinking.

questions.concept: Owning the customer relationship vs white-label distribution
questions.question: A fintech offering instant personal loans gets an offer: a large bank will distribute the loans under the bank's brand to its 50 million customers. Volumes would grow fast. What is the main long-term strategic risk to weigh?
options: The bank owns the customer relationship and data, so the fintech risks becoming a replaceable supplier
Loan volumes may grow faster than the fintech's servers can handle in the first few months
The bank's customers may have lower credit scores than the fintech's current users
Regulators may require extra paperwork for partnerships between banks and fintechs
questions.explanation: Under white-label distribution, customers know the bank, not the fintech. The bank keeps the relationship, the data and the ability to switch suppliers, so the fintech's bargaining power falls over time and margins get squeezed. The deal can still be worth it, but terms should protect data access, exclusivity or brand presence.
rationales: Correct: losing the customer relationship is the structural, long-term risk of white-label deals.
Scaling is an operational issue that can be planned for; it is not the strategic risk.
Credit quality matters but can be handled through underwriting rules in the contract.
Compliance work is a cost, not the main strategic threat to the business.
questions.interview_tip: Distribution-partnership questions test whether you understand who captures value. Strong candidates name relationship ownership and suggest contract terms that reduce the risk.

questions.concept: Cone of uncertainty in early estimates
questions.question: In a kickoff, an executive asks for a firm ship date for a new feature that has no design or technical spike yet. What is the best response?
options: Give the most optimistic date to show commitment and push the team to move faster
Give a wide range now and commit to narrowing it after design and a technical spike
Refuse to give any date until the full specification and design are complete
Ask engineering to pad their estimate by 50% and commit to that as a fixed date
questions.explanation: Estimates made before design and technical discovery are very uncertain, and that uncertainty narrows as work clarifies the unknowns. Sharing a range with a clear point at which it will tighten is honest and still useful for planning. It sets expectations without making a promise the team cannot keep.
rationales: Optimistic dates set the team up to miss and damage trust when reality arrives.
Correct: a range plus a plan to narrow it reflects real uncertainty and still supports planning.
Refusing any date blocks planning; leaders need a rough horizon even early on.
Arbitrary padding produces a fake precise date and hides the real uncertainty.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers listen for how you handle pressure for certainty. Explaining what will narrow the range, and when, shows execution maturity.

questions.concept: Decision memo with options and a recommendation
questions.question: Three teams disagree on whether to build an in-house payments flow or keep a third-party gateway. A VP will decide next week. What should the PM prepare?
options: A detailed spec of the in-house option, since it is the PM's preferred path
A slide listing each team's opinion so the VP can hear every side equally
A short memo with the decision, options, criteria, trade-offs and a clear recommendation
A survey of all engineers on the three teams asking which option they prefer
questions.explanation: A decision maker needs the question framed, the real options laid side by side against agreed criteria, and the PM's recommendation with reasoning. A decision memo does this, makes trade-offs explicit, and leaves a record of why the choice was made. Listing opinions or polling engineers pushes the analysis onto the VP.
rationales: Presenting only one option hides trade-offs and looks like advocacy rather than analysis.
A list of opinions without criteria or a recommendation leaves the VP to do the analysis.
Correct: it frames the choice, compares options fairly, and gives a reasoned recommendation.
Popularity among engineers is one input, not a decision method; it ignores cost and business risk.
questions.interview_tip: Amazon-style loops value written decision documents. Mentioning that you would surface the strongest case for the option you don't recommend is a strong signal.

questions.concept: Pre-built launch monitoring dashboard with alert thresholds
questions.question: Your team will roll out a new checkout flow next Monday. Which preparation is most important for launch-day monitoring?
options: Build a dashboard of key and guardrail metrics with alert thresholds and owners before launch
Plan to pull metrics with ad-hoc SQL queries if anyone reports problems during the day
Wait for the weekly business review to see how checkout conversion changed
Ask customer support to forward any complaints they receive about the new flow
questions.explanation: Problems in checkout cost money every minute, so the team needs to spot them fast and know who acts. A pre-built dashboard with thresholds and owners turns monitoring into a quick yes/no check. Support tickets and ad-hoc queries are useful but too slow as the main signal.
rationales: Correct: it makes problems visible quickly and makes clear who responds.
Ad-hoc queries are slow and error-prone under pressure, and only start after damage is noticed.
A weekly review is far too slow for a change that could break revenue on day one.
Complaints are a lagging and partial signal; most affected users simply leave.
questions.interview_tip: Launch questions reward candidates who define success and failure signals before shipping. Naming guardrails and owners shows operational readiness.

questions.concept: Owning a launch bug that overcharged customers
questions.question: A pricing change you specified shipped with an edge case that overcharged about 2,000 customers for three days. Engineering has a fix ready. What should you do first?
options: Ship the fix quietly and monitor, since raising it widely could create unnecessary panic
Explain to leadership that QA missed the edge case, so the process needs review
Wait until you have a full root-cause analysis before telling anyone outside the team
Ship the fix, tell your manager and stakeholders now, and drive refunds and an apology to affected customers
questions.explanation: Ownership means fixing the problem, making it visible quickly, and making customers whole. Telling stakeholders early lets support, finance and comms prepare, and proactive refunds protect trust. A blameless review can follow, but the first moves are fix, inform and remediate.
rationales: Hiding the issue risks a bigger trust and compliance problem when customers or finance find it.
Shifting blame to QA damages trust; the spec was yours and the team shares the outcome.
Delaying disclosure leaves support and finance unprepared and customers out of pocket.
Correct: it combines a quick fix, early transparency and putting customers first.
questions.interview_tip: Mistake stories are common in Amazon loops (Ownership, Earn Trust). Strong answers own the error without blame, describe the remedy for customers, and end with the process change.

questions.concept: Responding to burnout signs on your team before a deadline
questions.question: Two weeks before a major launch, your strongest engineer has been working late every night, is snapping in meetings and missed a review. What is the best action?
options: Leave it alone until after launch, since the team needs their output to hit the date
Talk to them privately, then work with their manager to cut or redistribute scope
Mention in stand-up that everyone should take care of themselves and avoid overwork
Escalate to their manager that their behaviour in meetings has become unprofessional
questions.explanation: Burnout is a people risk and a delivery risk: an exhausted key engineer is more likely to make mistakes or leave. A private, caring conversation shows respect, and working with their manager on scope addresses the cause rather than the symptom. PMs own scope trade-offs, so this is within their power.
rationales: Ignoring it risks errors, illness or attrition at the worst moment.
Correct: it addresses the person with care and fixes the workload that is causing the strain.
A general reminder doesn't change the workload and can feel dismissive to the person under pressure.
Framing it as misconduct punishes the symptom and ignores the overload behind it.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers want to see empathy and action, not just kindness. Pairing a one-to-one conversation with a concrete scope change is what a strong answer looks like.

questions.concept: Responding when sales promises an unplanned custom feature
questions.question: A sales director closed a large deal by promising a custom reporting feature within six weeks, without asking product. The roadmap is full. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Refuse the feature and tell sales they must go back to the customer and retract the promise
Add the feature to the next sprint to protect the deal, then raise the process issue later
Meet sales to understand the customer's real need, propose an option you can deliver, and agree how future commitments are made
Escalate to the CEO to decide whether sales or product owns the roadmap
questions.explanation: The deal and the relationship both matter. Understanding the customer's underlying need often reveals a smaller or existing solution that meets it, which protects the deal without derailing the roadmap. Agreeing a process for future commitments fixes the root cause without public blame.
rationales: A flat refusal may lose a large customer and damages the sales relationship.
Silently absorbing the work rewards the behaviour and pushes out other commitments without a decision.
Correct: it solves the customer's need, protects the roadmap, and fixes the process with sales as a partner.
Escalating first turns a solvable problem into a power struggle and should be a last resort.
questions.interview_tip: Stakeholder-conflict prompts test influence without authority. Strong answers dig into the real need, offer options and repair the process rather than win the argument.

questions.concept: Position bias in pairwise LLM-judge comparisons
questions.question: You use an LLM judge to compare two chatbot answers side by side and pick the better one. You notice it picks whichever answer appears first more often than expected. What is the simplest fix?
options: Run each comparison twice with the order swapped and only count consistent wins
Switch to a larger judge model, which will not have any ordering preference
Always put the new model's answer second so it never gets an unfair advantage
Ask the judge to give each answer a 1-10 score instead of picking a winner
questions.explanation: LLM judges can favour an answer because of where it appears in the prompt. Evaluating both orders and keeping only consistent verdicts (or averaging them) cancels this bias. It is cheap and keeps the pairwise format, which is often more reliable than absolute scores.
rationales: Correct: swapping order and requiring consistency removes the position effect.
Larger models can reduce bias but do not reliably remove it; you still need to control for order.
Fixing the order just builds the bias into every result, in a known direction.
Absolute scores have their own calibration problems and do not directly fix position bias.
questions.interview_tip: AI PM interviews increasingly probe eval design. Knowing common judge biases (position, verbosity, self-preference) and how to control them signals hands-on experience.

questions.concept: Limits of ROUGE for evaluating abstractive summaries
questions.question: Your team's new meeting-summary model scores lower on ROUGE than the old one, but users in a blind test prefer the new summaries. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Users in the test were biased toward the newer model because its summaries were longer
The new model must be hallucinating, since ROUGE is designed to detect factual errors
ROUGE rewards word overlap with a reference, so better summaries that paraphrase can score lower
The blind test was too small, so ROUGE should be trusted over the user preference
questions.explanation: ROUGE counts how many words and phrases overlap with a reference summary. A model that rephrases, condenses or organises information differently can be more useful yet share fewer words with the reference. That is why teams pair overlap metrics with human or rubric-based evaluation of usefulness and faithfulness.
rationales: Length bias can exist, but nothing suggests the summaries were longer; it is speculation.
ROUGE does not check facts; it only measures word overlap.
Correct: overlap metrics penalise valid paraphrasing that humans find clearer.
Without evidence the test was underpowered, the mismatch more likely reveals the metric's limits.
questions.interview_tip: Show you know which metrics measure what. Strong candidates explain why automatic metrics and user preference can disagree and how they would combine them.

questions.concept: Checking that cited sources actually support each claim
questions.question: An AI research assistant answers with footnoted citations. Audits find that 15% of footnotes link to real pages that do not actually support the sentence they're attached to. What is the most effective fix?
options: Show more citations per sentence so users have several sources to cross-check
Add a check that each cited passage supports its claim, and drop or rewrite claims that fail
Add a disclaimer telling users that citations may not always be accurate
Restrict retrieval to well-known domains so all cited pages are trustworthy
questions.explanation: The failure is not fake links but mismatched support: the page exists, but it doesn't say what the sentence claims. A claim-to-passage verification step, often done with a second model or entailment check, catches these before users see them. Trustworthy domains don't help if the cited passage still says something different.
rationales: More citations add noise and don't fix the mismatch between claims and sources.
Correct: verifying support for each claim targets the exact failure the audit found.
A disclaimer shifts the burden to users and doesn't improve accuracy.
Reputable sources can still be cited for claims they don't make; trust in the domain isn't support for the claim.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like candidates who diagnose the precise failure mode before proposing a fix. Separating 'fake citation' from 'unsupported claim' shows depth.

questions.concept: Evaluating agent trajectories, not just final answers
questions.question: Your customer-service agent can issue refunds through a tool. Final-answer accuracy on the eval set is 94%, yet production reviews find refunds issued without the required order check. What is the eval missing?
options: A larger eval set, since 94% accuracy on a small set may not be statistically reliable
A user-satisfaction survey after every conversation to catch unhappy customers
A comparison against a stronger model to see whether its final answers score higher
Checks on the agent's sequence of tool calls, such as whether it verified the order before refunding
questions.explanation: An agent can reach an acceptable final reply through an unsafe or non-compliant path. Trajectory evaluation inspects the steps: which tools were called, in what order and with what arguments, against required policies. For agents that take real actions, process checks matter as much as outcome checks.
rationales: More examples improve confidence but still only grade final answers, so they would miss the skipped step.
Customers who get refunds are often satisfied, so surveys wouldn't reveal the policy violation.
A stronger model's final answers don't tell you whether either agent follows the required process.
Correct: grading the tool-call sequence catches policy violations that final-answer scoring misses.
questions.interview_tip: Agent eval is a hot topic in AI PM loops. Strong answers distinguish outcome from process metrics and tie them to business risk such as unauthorised refunds.

questions.concept: Usage quotas to control cost and abuse of a free AI feature
questions.question: A free AI image-editing feature costs about ₹2 per edit. A small share of users run thousands of edits a day, some via scripts. What should the PM introduce first?
options: Per-user daily quotas with rate limits, plus higher limits on a paid plan
Remove the feature from the free plan entirely to stop all the cost at once
Switch to a cheaper model for everyone, accepting a drop in output quality
Add a CAPTCHA before every single edit to block scripted usage
questions.explanation: A long tail of heavy or automated users can drive most of the cost of a free AI feature. Daily quotas and rate limits cap the exposure while keeping the feature generous for normal users, and a paid tier turns genuine heavy demand into revenue. It is a targeted fix rather than a blanket penalty.
rationales: Correct: it caps cost from outliers, blocks scripts, and creates an upgrade path for real power users.
Removing the feature punishes all normal users to stop a small minority.
A cheaper model lowers quality for everyone while abusers keep running unlimited edits.
A CAPTCHA on every edit adds friction for all users and determined scripts can often get past it.
questions.interview_tip: AI cost questions test whether you target the source of cost. Mentioning that a quota can double as a monetisation lever is a strong signal.

questions.concept: App-store release lag and forced-update constraints for mobile fixes
questions.question: A bug in your mobile app's latest version shows wrong prices on one screen. The web version was fixed in minutes. Why is the mobile fix harder, and what helps most next time?
options: Mobile code is harder to write; hiring more mobile engineers would speed up fixes
Mobile apps can't be changed after release; only a full reinstall fixes any bug
Updates need store review and users update slowly; server-driven config and feature flags let you change behaviour without a release
Mobile bugs are rare, so the best plan is simply more manual testing before each release
questions.explanation: A mobile release must pass app-store review, and even after approval many users stay on old versions for weeks. Logic and content that are served from the backend, or guarded by remote flags, can be changed instantly for all versions. Forced-update prompts are a last resort for critical issues.
rationales: More engineers don't remove store review or slow user adoption of updates.
Apps can be updated through new releases and remote config; a reinstall is not required.
Correct: it names the real constraint and the standard way around it.
Testing helps, but bugs will still ship; the issue is how fast you can fix them.
questions.interview_tip: Technical fluency rounds check whether you understand delivery constraints that shape product decisions. Mentioning remote config and kill switches shows practical experience.

questions.concept: Verifying webhook authenticity with signatures
questions.question: Your app receives 'payment succeeded' webhooks from a payment provider and then marks orders as paid. A security review flags a risk. What is the most important protection?
options: Make the webhook endpoint URL long and random so nobody can guess it
Verify each webhook's signature using the provider's shared secret before acting on it
Only accept webhooks that arrive within a few seconds of the payment attempt
Log every webhook request so you can investigate suspicious payments later
questions.explanation: Anyone who discovers your endpoint could send a fake 'payment succeeded' message. Payment providers sign each webhook with a secret only you and they share, so verifying the signature proves it is genuine and unchanged. Timestamp checks help against replays, but they come in addition to signatures, not instead of them.
rationales: A hidden URL is security by obscurity; URLs leak through logs and config.
Correct: signature verification proves the message came from the provider and wasn't altered.
Timing checks can help stop replays but don't prove who sent the message.
Logging helps investigations after the fact but does not stop fake orders being marked paid.
questions.interview_tip: Expect simple security scenarios in technical rounds. Strong answers name the threat (forged requests) and the standard control (signature verification).

questions.concept: Lower retention of festive-sale acquisition cohorts
questions.question: An Indian e-commerce app acquired a record 3 million new users during a festive sale with deep discounts. Three months later, their repeat-purchase rate is half that of users acquired in normal months. What is the best interpretation?
options: The app's post-sale experience got worse, so all recent cohorts are churning faster
Festive users were acquired by discounts, so judge them on their own cohort LTV and design follow-ups for them
The sale was a mistake and should be dropped next year because the users don't stick
Normal-month users must be lying in surveys about their intent to repeat purchase
questions.explanation: Users acquired with deep discounts are often more price-driven and less likely to repeat at full price, so their cohort behaves differently. That doesn't make the sale a failure; it means acquisition spend should be judged on that cohort's own LTV against its cost. Tailored follow-ups, such as targeted second-purchase offers, can lift their retention.
rationales: If the experience got worse, normal-month cohorts would decline too; the gap points to who was acquired.
Correct: it recognises cohort quality differs by acquisition context and plans around it.
One weak metric doesn't make the sale unprofitable; it needs cohort LTV against acquisition cost.
Surveys are irrelevant; the comparison is based on actual purchase behaviour.
questions.interview_tip: Growth interviews reward cohort thinking: segmenting by acquisition source or context before drawing conclusions. Linking it to LTV/CAC shows commercial sense.

questions.concept: GitHub Copilot Fusion cascade routing (Oct 2026)
questions.question: GitHub made Copilot Fusion generally available on 28 October 2026. In its 'Cascade' workflow, how does Fusion handle a prompt?
options: It sends the prompt to every enabled model in parallel and returns the answer most models agree on
A lower-cost model drafts a response, and a quality check decides whether to accept it or escalate to a stronger model
One model drafts a response, a second model reviews it, and the first model revises its answer
The user picks one model per task, and Fusion only switches models if that model's API is down
questions.explanation: GitHub's changelog describes three Fusion workflows: Single, Cascade and Critique. In Cascade, a cheaper model drafts first, and a quality check either accepts the draft or escalates to a stronger model. This is a classic cost-quality routing pattern: most tasks get handled cheaply, and only hard ones pay for the expensive model. Users are billed for each model Fusion uses at its standard rate.
rationales: Parallel voting across all models isn't one of the workflows GitHub described, and it would multiply cost.
Correct: this matches GitHub's description of the Cascade workflow.
This describes Fusion's separate 'Critique' workflow, not Cascade.
With Fusion, users choose an effort level rather than a model; this describes failover, not routing.
questions.interview_tip: Model routing is a common AI product strategy topic. Be ready to explain the cost-quality trade-off of cascades and what the quality check must catch for escalation to work.
